title: Spider web rose (ribbon)
subtitle: Five straight-stitch spokes woven with silk ribbon to build a full ribbon rose
excerpt: A spider web rose in silk ribbon starts with five evenly spaced straight-stitch spokes radiating from a central point. Silk ribbon is then woven over and under the spokes in a spiral from the centre outward until the spokes are fully covered and the rose is full.
sourceNotes: Woven rose foundation technique documented in 19th-century needlework manuals including Weldon's Practical Needlework series. Spider web rose adapted for silk ribbon embroidery as standard in 20th-century ribbon embroidery references.

content.text: The spider web rose is the best-known ribbon embroidery technique. Five straight-stitch spokes in ordinary embroidery thread provide the structure, and silk ribbon is then woven over and under the spokes in a spiralling path outward from the centre. As the ribbon builds up, it compresses slightly and the folds create the layered look of rose petals. The finished rose is rounded, raised, and full, all from a five-spoke wheel.

items.label: Ribbon
items.value: 7 mm pure silk ribbon for a full rose; 4 mm for a small bud; colour can graduate from dark at the centre to light at the outer petals

items.label: Fabric
items.value: Firm cotton, silk, or linen mounted tightly in a hoop

items.label: Needle
items.value: Embroidery needle size 9 or 10 for the spoke stitches; chenille needle size 16 or 18 for the ribbon weaving

items.label: Hoop
items.value: 15 cm embroidery hoop; taut fabric prevents the spokes from pulling when the ribbon is woven

content.text: Thread the embroidery needle with two strands of stranded cotton in a colour that will be hidden by the ribbon. Work five straight stitches radiating from a single central hole, spacing them evenly. The outer end of each spoke should fall on the edge of the planned rose circle. All five spokes share the same centre hole.

Thread the chenille needle with a 35 to 40 cm length of silk ribbon. Bring it up through the fabric close to the centre hole but not through the centre itself. Keep the ribbon untwisted as it comes up.

Slide the needle under one spoke and over the next, then under the following spoke and over the one after that. Use the blunt side of the needle or a tapestry needle to weave so you do not split the spoke threads. Keep the ribbon flat and untwisted as you weave.

Continue spiralling outward, over one spoke and under the next, allowing the ribbon to twist and fold slightly as it progresses. Do not pull tight: the folds create the petal texture. Keep the tension relaxed so the ribbon billows.

When all five spokes are covered to their tips and the rose is the desired fullness, take the ribbon down through the fabric close to the outer edge of the rose. Secure it at the back with a few stitches in ordinary thread.

attrs.heading: When the spider web rose goes wrong

items.symptom: The rose looks flat and uniform rather than having petal depth
items.cause: The ribbon is pulled too tight as it weaves, or not enough ribbon is used to fill the spokes.
items.fix: Keep the tension loose. Let each loop of ribbon sit naturally without pulling it down against the fabric. If the spokes run out before the rose looks full, restart the weaving with a new length of ribbon, bringing it up close to where the last length ended.

items.symptom: The spoke threads show between the ribbon loops
items.cause: The spokes are too long for the amount of ribbon used, or the ribbon is too narrow for the rose size.
items.fix: Use a wider ribbon (7 mm rather than 4 mm) or shorten the spoke length. The ribbon should cover the spokes completely by the time it reaches the spoke tips.

items.symptom: The ribbon splits or frays as it is drawn through the fabric
items.cause: The chenille needle is too small for the ribbon width, or the needle eye is catching the ribbon edge.
items.fix: Use a chenille needle one size larger. The eye must be wide enough for the ribbon to pass without folding or catching.
